opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important principle is putting the user first, or more concretely, being obsessed with creating real value for the people who use Meshy.

It sounds simple, and every company says something like it, but in practice it's very easy to drift away from. As engineers, and especially coming from a research background like mine, there's a strong temptation to build things because they're technically interesting or impressive. In graphics and AI there's always a cooler algorithm or a fancier demo. But a demo that looks great on Twitter doesn't necessarily help a game developer ship their game faster, or help a 3D artist get through a tedious part of their workflow.

So internally we keep asking: who is this for, and what problem does it actually solve for them? We talk to users a lot, watch how they use the product, and look at where they get stuck. Often the most valuable improvement isn't a new model at all. It might be better topology, a cleaner export to a game engine, or making generation a few seconds faster. Those things aren't glamorous, but they matter a lot to people using the tool every day.

Closely tied to that is speed of iteration. Generative AI moves incredibly fast, and the landscape changes every few months. If you spend half a year polishing something in isolation, the world may have moved on by the time you release it. We'd rather ship, learn from real feedback, and improve quickly. Being user-centric and moving fast reinforce each other: the faster you iterate, the faster you learn what users actually need.

And underneath both, I'd say ownership. In a small team, everyone needs to care about the outcome, not just their own piece. When people feel responsible for whether the user is happy, rather than just whether their task is closed, the whole company moves in the right direction without needing a lot of process.

So if I had to sum it up in one sentence: build things people genuinely need, and get them into their hands as quickly as possible.

r001.rationale: The response names user focus, fast iteration, and ownership as cultural principles, but does not identify pragmatism or explicitly describe respecting facts and facing reality as the cornerstone.

r002.rationale: It does not say that many mistakes come from failing to look at reality objectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. If I had to pick one principle, it would be what we call "ship fast, but don't ship junk." At Meshy, speed is in our DNA. The generative 3D space moves incredibly quickly, and if we spend six months perfecting something in isolation, the world has already moved on. So we push ourselves to get things into users' hands early and learn from real feedback.

But speed alone isn't enough. A lot of my background is in research, where you're trained to be rigorous and skeptical of your own results. We try to carry that into the company. When we put out a new model or feature, we want it to actually work for the artists and developers relying on it, not just look good in a demo. So there's a constant tension between moving fast and holding a high bar, and I think living in that tension is what keeps us healthy.

Underneath that is a lot of trust and ownership. We hire people who care deeply about their craft, give them real problems, and get out of the way. If everyone owns their piece and talks honestly about what's working and what isn't, you don't need heavy process to move quickly. That's the culture I'm trying to protect as we grow.

r001.rationale: The candidate names “ship fast, but don’t ship junk” as the principle and mentions real feedback and rigor, but does not identify pragmatism or facing reality as the cornerstone.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not attribute mistakes to failing to look at reality objectively.

astra-6.text: I think the most important principle is taking ownership. That means understanding the problem we’re trying to solve, thinking independently, and taking responsibility for the outcome. If something isn’t working, we want people to feel comfortable saying so and proposing a better approach. That helps the whole team learn and move forward.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the most important principle is focusing on the user. In generative AI, it’s easy to get excited about the technology itself, but what matters is whether it helps someone create what they have in mind. That means listening carefully, learning from how people actually use Meshy, and being willing to change our assumptions.
